notice: RN bank batch 26: Maternity I: antepartum care and complications. Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: At a first prenatal visit, a 27-year-old client with regular 28-day cycles says the last menstrual period began on December 24, 2026. The client also had light spotting on January 7, 2027, and asks whether that changes the due date. Using Naegele's rule, which estimated date of birth should the nurse document?

options.text: September 30, 2027
September 24, 2027
October 14, 2027
March 31, 2027

rationale.correct: Naegele's rule: first day of the last normal menstrual period + 7 days − 3 months + 1 year.

perOption.a: December 24 + 7 days = December 31; minus 3 months = September 30; plus 1 year = 2027. Spotting after the LMP is not used.
perOption.b: This leaves out the 7 days.
perOption.c: This dates the pregnancy from the spotting, which is often implantation bleeding, not a period.
perOption.d: This adds 3 months instead of subtracting them.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate an estimated date of birth.

questions.stem: A client at 18 weeks gestation asks the nurse whether the pregnancy is "definitely real" after a friend said home tests can be wrong. The chart lists several findings from today's visit. Which finding is a positive (certain) sign of pregnancy?

options.text: Fetal heart tones of 150/min heard with a Doppler
Ballottement of the fetus felt during the pelvic exam
Quickening first felt by the client at 17 weeks
A serum hCG level of 45,000 mIU/mL

rationale.correct: Positive signs: fetal heart tones, fetal movement felt by the examiner and the fetus seen on ultrasound.

perOption.a: Signs that come directly from the fetus are the only positive signs.
perOption.b: Ballottement is a probable sign; a uterine polyp or mass can rebound in the same way.
perOption.c: Movement felt by the client is presumptive; gas can feel the same.
perOption.d: hCG is a probable sign; it can rise with a molar pregnancy or some tumors.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A pregnant client's history: a son born at 41 weeks who is now 6, a stillbirth at 23 weeks, twins born at 35 weeks who are both living, and a miscarriage at 8 weeks. The nurse is recording the obstetric history using GTPAL. Which entry is correct?

options.text: G5 T1 P2 A1 L3
G5 T1 P1 A2 L3
G4 T1 P2 A1 L3
G5 T1 P3 A1 L3

rationale.correct: GTPAL: Gravida, Term (37 weeks or more), Preterm (20 to 36 6/7 weeks, living or not), Abortions (before 20 weeks), Living. Multiples count once for G, T and P.

perOption.a: 5 pregnancies including this one; 1 term birth; 2 preterm births (the stillbirth after 20 weeks and the twins, counted once); 1 abortion; 3 living children.
perOption.b: A loss at 23 weeks is past 20 weeks, so it counts as a preterm birth, not an abortion.
perOption.c: The current pregnancy counts toward gravida.
perOption.d: Twins count as one birth for term and preterm.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old client who plans to become pregnant in the next few months had a previous pregnancy affected by spina bifida. The client takes no medicines and eats a balanced diet. Which recommendation should the nurse expect the provider to make?

options.text: Folic acid 4 mg daily, starting at least 1 month before trying to conceive
Folic acid 400 mcg daily, starting as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
A prenatal vitamin with 10,000 IU of vitamin A to support development
Diet alone, because a varied, balanced diet supplies enough folate for pregnancy

rationale.correct: Folic acid: 400 mcg daily for most; 4 mg daily after a previous neural tube defect, from at least 1 month before conception through the first trimester.

perOption.a: A previous neural tube defect calls for the high dose of folic acid, started before conception.
perOption.b: The neural tube closes by about 4 weeks, often before pregnancy is known, and this client needs the higher dose.
perOption.c: High-dose vitamin A is teratogenic.
perOption.d: Supplements are recommended for all who could become pregnant.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks gestation says they wake at night with a painful cramp in the calf. Both calves are equal in size, soft and not warm. What should the nurse suggest the client do when a cramp starts?

options.text: Straighten the knee and pull the toes up toward the shin
Point the toes down firmly until the cramp goes away
Take an extra calcium tablet at the time of the cramp
Lie flat with the legs raised on two pillows

rationale.correct: Leg cramps: dorsiflexion, calf stretches before bed, fluids and adequate calcium and magnesium.

perOption.a: Dorsiflexion stretches the calf muscle and relieves the cramp.
perOption.b: Plantar flexion shortens the calf and can worsen the cramp.
perOption.c: Calcium does not stop a cramp in progress.
perOption.d: This does not stretch the muscle.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks gestation lying flat on the back for an ultrasound says, "I feel faint." The client is pale and sweaty, the blood pressure has fallen from 118/72 to 88/50 mm Hg, and the pulse is 112/min. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Turn the client onto the left side
Raise the legs and lower the head of the table
Apply oxygen at 10 L/min by nonrebreather mask
Check a fingerstick blood glucose level

rationale.correct: Supine hypotensive syndrome: lateral (preferably left) positioning or a wedge under the right hip.

perOption.a: This lifts the uterus off the vena cava and restores venous return (supine hypotensive syndrome).
perOption.b: The uterus still compresses the vena cava in this position.
perOption.c: Relieving the compression comes first.
perOption.d: The timing and position point to a positional cause.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client at 26 weeks gestation which symptoms need a call to the provider the same day, rather than waiting for the next routine visit. Which symptoms should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Puffiness of the face and hands that is present on waking
A gush or steady trickle of clear fluid from the vagina
Burning on urination with a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F)
Fewer fetal movements than usual over the day
Irregular, painless tightening that eases with rest and fluids
Thin, white vaginal discharge without odor or itching
Ankle swelling at the end of the day that is gone by morning

rationale.correct: Danger signs: bleeding, fluid leakage, headache or vision changes, facial or hand edema, fever, painful urination, decreased movement and regular contractions before 37 weeks.

perOption.a: Facial and hand edema can be an early sign of preeclampsia.
perOption.b: This may be rupture of membranes.
perOption.c: A urinary infection with fever raises the risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labor.
perOption.d: Decreased movement can signal fetal compromise.
perOption.g: Dependent edema that resolves overnight is common.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At a first prenatal visit at 10 weeks, a client who is 165 cm tall and weighed 74 kg before pregnancy (BMI 27) asks how much weight to gain with this single pregnancy. Which total gain should the nurse recommend?

options.text: 7 to 11.5 kg (15 to 25 lb)
11.5 to 16 kg (25 to 35 lb)
5 to 9 kg (11 to 20 lb)
12.5 to 18 kg (28 to 40 lb)

rationale.correct: Weight gain goals depend on pre-pregnancy BMI: underweight 28 to 40 lb, normal 25 to 35 lb, overweight 15 to 25 lb, obese 11 to 20 lb.

perOption.a: This is the recommendation for an overweight BMI of 25 to 29.9.
perOption.b: This is for a normal BMI of 18.5 to 24.9.
perOption.c: This is for an obese BMI of 30 or more.
perOption.d: This is for an underweight BMI below 18.5.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at a first prenatal visit at 9 weeks has a BMI of 34, had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy and has a parent with type 2 diabetes. When should the nurse expect this client to be screened for diabetes?

options.text: At this visit, and again at 24 to 28 weeks if the result is normal
At 24 to 28 weeks, the standard time for screening in pregnancy
At 32 weeks, once insulin resistance reaches its peak
At the 6-week postpartum visit, before any future pregnancy is planned

rationale.correct: Screen for diabetes at 24 to 28 weeks; screen at the first visit when risk factors such as obesity or previous gestational diabetes are present.

perOption.a: Clients with risk factors are screened early and, if negative, again at the usual time.
perOption.b: This client's risk factors call for early screening as well.
perOption.c: This is too late to treat and prevent fetal effects.
perOption.d: Postpartum testing is also needed, but it does not replace screening now.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks with gestational diabetes has fasting glucose readings of 110 to 125 mg/dL despite diet changes and asks how the high readings could affect the baby. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The baby may grow large and have low blood sugar after birth."
"The baby may be small, because your insulin does not reach the baby."
"The baby is likely to be born with diabetes that needs insulin."
"The baby may have high blood sugar for the first few days."

rationale.correct: Gestational diabetes: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia, respiratory distress and hyperbilirubinemia.

perOption.a: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta; fetal insulin rises, causing macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia after the glucose supply stops.
perOption.b: Insulin does not cross the placenta; glucose does, and the fetus makes extra insulin.
perOption.c: Gestational diabetes does not cause diabetes in the newborn.
perOption.d: Newborns of diabetic mothers are at risk of low blood sugar.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain fetal risks of gestational diabetes.

questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks whose blood pressure was 112/70 mm Hg at 12 weeks now has a blood pressure of 164/112 mm Hg on two readings 15 minutes apart, a headache not relieved by acetaminophen and spots before the eyes. Urine protein is 2+. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Preeclampsia with severe features
Gestational hypertension without proteinuria
Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia
Eclampsia

rationale.correct: Severe features: BP 160/110 or higher, persistent headache, vision changes, RUQ pain, platelets below 100,000, raised liver enzymes, pulmonary edema or rising creatinine.

perOption.a: New hypertension after 20 weeks with severe-range readings and neurologic symptoms meets the criteria.
perOption.b: Proteinuria and symptoms are present.
perOption.c: The blood pressure was normal early in pregnancy, so there is no chronic hypertension.
perOption.d: Eclampsia requires a seizure.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with preeclampsia is receiving IV magnesium sulfate at 2 g/hr. On hourly assessment, the client is drowsy, the respiratory rate is 10/min, the patellar reflexes are absent and the urine output was 20 mL over the past hour. Calcium gluconate is at the bedside. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion
Give calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 3 minutes
Draw a serum magnesium level and call the provider
Increase the IV fluid rate to improve urine output

rationale.correct: Magnesium: keep RR at 12/min or more, reflexes present, urine output 30 mL/hr or more and the client alert. The antidote is calcium gluconate.

perOption.a: These signs show magnesium toxicity; the infusion is stopped first so that no more drug is given, then calcium gluconate and the provider.
perOption.b: The antidote is given next, but the infusion is still running and must be stopped first.
perOption.c: This delays treatment of clear toxicity.
perOption.d: Fluid overload risks pulmonary edema in preeclampsia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 33 weeks with preeclampsia reports nausea and pain under the right ribs. Laboratory results: platelets 85,000/mm3, AST 210 units/L, ALT 190 units/L, LDH 780 units/L and schistocytes on the blood smear. Glucose is 92 mg/dL. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: HELLP syndrome
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Acute cholecystitis
Immune thrombocytopenia

rationale.correct: HELLP is a severe form of preeclampsia; stabilize, give magnesium and plan for delivery.

perOption.a: Hemolysis (LDH, schistocytes), elevated liver enzymes and low platelets.
perOption.b: This usually causes low glucose and liver failure without the hemolysis picture.
perOption.c: This does not explain hemolysis or low platelets.
perOption.d: This lowers platelets but does not raise liver enzymes or cause hemolysis.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two clients at 32 weeks are admitted with vaginal bleeding. For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with placenta previa or placental abruption.

rows.text: Bright red bleeding that started during sleep without pain
A rigid, tender uterus between contractions
Fundal height that has risen 2 cm since admission
Late decelerations with a small amount of visible bleeding
Fetus in a transverse lie on ultrasound

rationale.correct: Previa: painless, bright red, soft uterus, no vaginal exams. Abruption: painful, rigid uterus, concealed bleeding, early fetal distress.

perOption.r1:c1: Previa typically causes painless bright red bleeding.
perOption.r2:c1: The uterus stays soft in previa.
perOption.r2:c2: Blood behind the placenta irritates the uterus, making it rigid and tender.
perOption.r3:c1: Uterine scarring raises the risk of a low-lying placenta.
perOption.r3:c2: Scarring is more strongly linked with previa.
perOption.r4:c1: Previa bleeding is visible, not trapped.
perOption.r4:c2: Concealed bleeding behind the placenta enlarges the uterus.
perOption.r5:c1: Previa usually causes no fetal distress unless bleeding is heavy.
perOption.r5:c2: Separation reduces placental blood flow, even when little blood is seen.
perOption.r6:c1: A low placenta keeps the head from settling into the pelvis.
perOption.r6:c2: Abnormal lie is not typical of abruption.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks gestation is admitted with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding. The fetal heart rate is 145/min with moderate variability, and no ultrasound has been done yet. Which admission order should the nurse question?

options.text: Sterile vaginal exam to check cervical dilation
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring
Insert a large-bore IV and send a type and screen
Weigh perineal pads to measure blood loss

rationale.correct: Suspected previa: no vaginal or rectal exams until ultrasound shows where the placenta is.

perOption.a: An exam can tear a low-lying placenta and cause hemorrhage.
perOption.b: This is needed to watch fetal status.
perOption.c: This prepares for possible hemorrhage.
perOption.d: This measures bleeding accurately.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Avoid vaginal exams with suspected previa.

questions.stem: A client at 7 weeks gestation by dates comes to the emergency department with sharp left lower abdominal pain, light spotting and new pain in the right shoulder. The pulse is 118/min and the blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Threatened spontaneous abortion
Ruptured ovarian corpus luteum cyst
Acute appendicitis

rationale.correct: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is an emergency: large-bore IV, type and crossmatch and preparation for surgery.

perOption.a: Shoulder pain suggests blood in the abdomen irritating the diaphragm, and the vital signs show hypovolemia.
perOption.b: This causes spotting and cramping, but not shoulder pain or shock.
perOption.c: This can bleed, but a tubal rupture must be ruled out first in a client this unstable.
perOption.d: Appendicitis is usually right-sided and does not cause spotting.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 10 weeks gestation has vomited several times a day for a week, cannot keep fluids down, has lost 6% of body weight and has 3+ ketones in the urine. The pulse is 108/min. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: IV fluids with electrolytes and thiamine, and an antiemetic
Reassurance that morning sickness eases by the second trimester
A clear liquid diet at home and a follow-up visit in 1 week
Large meals high in fat to replace the lost calories

rationale.correct: Hyperemesis: IV fluids, electrolytes, thiamine, antiemetics, then small frequent meals once tolerated.

perOption.a: Hyperemesis gravidarum causes dehydration and ketosis; thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.
perOption.b: Weight loss and ketonuria are not normal morning sickness.
perOption.c: The client cannot keep fluids down and needs treatment now.
perOption.d: Fatty meals worsen nausea; small, frequent bland meals are used once tolerated.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative client at 28 weeks has a negative indirect Coombs test. The client's first baby was Rh-positive, and the client received Rho(D) immune globulin after that birth. The client asks, "Do I need another shot?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Yes, a dose now, and again after birth if the baby is Rh-positive."
"No, the dose you had after your first birth protects later pregnancies."
"No, it is given only if your antibody screen turns positive."
"Yes, but it is given to your baby right after birth."

rationale.correct: Rho(D) immune globulin: at 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth of an Rh-positive infant, and after bleeding, trauma or invasive procedures, in every pregnancy.

perOption.a: Each pregnancy needs its own doses; the negative screen shows the client is not yet sensitized.
perOption.b: The immune globulin clears in weeks; it is given again with each pregnancy.
perOption.c: Once antibodies form, the immune globulin no longer helps.
perOption.d: It is given to the Rh-negative mother, not the newborn.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks with chronic hypertension has a 20-minute nonstress test. The baseline is 145/min with moderate variability, and the fetal heart rate rises 10 beats/min for 10 seconds twice with fetal movement. There are no decelerations. How should the nurse interpret this test?

options.text: Reactive, because the criteria before 32 weeks are met
Nonreactive, because the accelerations are under 15 beats for 15 seconds
Nonreactive, so a contraction stress test is needed right away
Inconclusive, so the test should be extended to 40 minutes

rationale.correct: NST: reactive = 2 or more accelerations in 20 minutes, 15 beats for 15 seconds at 32 weeks or more, or 10 beats for 10 seconds before 32 weeks.

perOption.a: Before 32 weeks, two accelerations of 10 beats for 10 seconds in 20 minutes is reactive.
perOption.b: The 15-by-15 criteria apply at 32 weeks or more.
perOption.c: The test is reactive at this gestational age.
perOption.d: Extending the test is done when criteria are not met in 20 minutes.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 16 weeks gestation is going home after an amniocentesis for genetic testing. Which statement by the client shows that the discharge teaching was understood?

options.text: "I'll call if I have cramping, fluid leaking or a fever."
"I'll expect some leaking of clear fluid for a day or two."
"I can go back to my running program as soon as I get home."
"I'll take aspirin if the puncture site feels sore tonight."

rationale.correct: After amniocentesis, report bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or contractions; Rh-negative clients receive Rho(D) immune globulin.

perOption.a: These may signal preterm labor, rupture of membranes or infection.
perOption.b: Fluid leakage is not expected and needs to be reported.
perOption.c: Strenuous activity is avoided for about a day.
perOption.d: Aspirin raises the risk of bleeding; acetaminophen is used.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in preterm labor at 30 weeks receives the first of two doses of betamethasone 12 mg IM, 24 hours apart. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding of the medicine?

options.text: "It helps the baby's lungs and works best if birth is 1 to 7 days away."
"It relaxes my uterus, so the contractions should slow down and stop soon."
"It protects my baby from an infection I might have."
"It works right away, so the baby is safe if born tonight."

rationale.correct: Betamethasone at 24 to 34 weeks: two doses 24 hours apart to mature fetal lungs; monitor maternal glucose.

perOption.a: Antenatal steroids reduce respiratory distress; the benefit is greatest 24 hours to 7 days after the first dose.
perOption.b: Tocolytics such as nifedipine slow contractions; steroids do not.
perOption.c: Antibiotics, such as for group B strep, do that.
perOption.d: Full benefit takes about 24 hours from the first dose.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 33 weeks reports a sudden gush of clear fluid 1 hour ago and a steady trickle since. A sterile speculum exam shows fluid pooling in the vagina, nitrazine paper turns blue and a dried sample shows ferning under the microscope. What do these findings suggest?

options.text: Preterm premature rupture of membranes
Stress incontinence from the weight of the uterus
Increased normal vaginal discharge of pregnancy
Bacterial vaginosis with a watery discharge

rationale.correct: Preterm premature rupture of membranes raises the risk of infection and preterm birth; confirm with pooling, nitrazine and ferning.

perOption.a: Pooling, an alkaline pH and ferning confirm amniotic fluid.
perOption.b: Urine is usually acidic and does not fern.
perOption.c: Vaginal discharge is acidic and does not fern.
perOption.d: This causes a fishy odor; it can raise the pH but does not fern.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At a first prenatal visit at 8 weeks, a client says they drank wine at a party before knowing they were pregnant. After teaching about alcohol in pregnancy, which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "No amount of alcohol is known to be safe while I'm pregnant."
"A glass of wine with dinner a few nights a week is fine."
"Beer and wine are safe; it's liquor that harms the baby."
"Alcohol is safe once the baby's organs have formed after 12 weeks."

rationale.correct: Avoid alcohol completely in pregnancy; a past exposure is discussed without blame and the client is encouraged to stop now.

perOption.a: Alcohol crosses the placenta and can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders at any stage.
perOption.b: No safe amount of alcohol is known.
perOption.c: All types of alcohol carry the same risk.
perOption.d: The brain keeps developing throughout pregnancy.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: At a prenatal visit, a client at 28 weeks by a first-trimester ultrasound has a fundal height of 34 cm. Two weeks ago it was 30 cm. The client feels well and the blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: An ultrasound, because the uterus is larger than expected for dates
Routine care, because fundal height often varies by a few centimeters
A new due date, because the dates are probably wrong
Bed rest, because the fundus is rising too quickly

rationale.correct: From 20 to 36 weeks, fundal height in cm roughly equals the weeks of gestation (± 2 cm).

perOption.a: A fundal height more than 2 cm above the weeks of gestation needs evaluation for macrosomia, polyhydramnios or multiples.
perOption.b: A 6 cm difference is outside the expected range.
perOption.c: A first-trimester ultrasound is the most accurate dating.
perOption.d: The cause must be found before a plan is made.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks gestation with a history of a stillbirth asks how to keep track of the baby's movements at home. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Count until you feel 10 movements; call if that takes over 2 hours."
"Count the movements once a week on the same day."
"Expect fewer movements from now on, as the baby has less room to move."
"Call if you notice no movement for a whole day."

rationale.correct: Fetal movement counts: report fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours.

perOption.a: Daily kick counts are a simple check of fetal well-being.
perOption.b: Daily counts are recommended.
perOption.c: Movements should not decrease; a decrease needs evaluation.
perOption.d: This is far too long to wait.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
